description: Deterministic current-law transfer, supersession, and cross-reference notes needed to reconcile CLARA, the Commerce Dispersal Act, and the Employment Clarity and Federal Workforce Modernization Act of 2026 with the baseline U.S. Code text. These notes do not rewrite historical OLRC text unless Congress expressly amended that Code text.

authorities.31-226: Commerce and Labor Administrative Reform Act (CLARA)
authorities.38-265: Employment Clarity and Federal Workforce Modernization Act of 2026

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Department of Commerce and Labor
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(a), enacted after Pub. L. 31–226 (CLARA), provides that the Department of Commerce and Labor shall be rendered inoperable and that its functions and duties are transferred in accordance with the Commerce Dispersal Act.

Pub. L. 36–256 did not expressly strike or replace 5 U.S.C. § 101. The Department therefore remains in the printed executive-department list as enacted text, but its current functions are governed by Pub. L. 36–256, §§ 3–4.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Federal Trade Commission
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(g), transfers the functions of the Federal Trade Commission as absorbed into the Department of Commerce and Labor to the Department of Justice in a manner prescribed by the Attorney General, and transfers corresponding empowerment of the Secretary of Commerce and Labor to the Attorney General.
The preexisting Federal Trade Commission text in this chapter is retained as enacted text; current USAR administration of the transferred functions is controlled by Pub. L. 36–256.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—National Labor Relations Board
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(h), transfers the functions of the National Labor Relations Board as absorbed into the Department of Commerce and Labor to the Department of Justice in a manner prescribed by the Attorney General, and transfers corresponding empowerment of the Secretary of Commerce and Labor to the Attorney General.
The preexisting National Labor Relations Board text in this subchapter is retained as enacted text; current USAR administration of the transferred functions is controlled by Pub. L. 36–256.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Federal Communications Commission
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(f), transfers the functions of the Federal Communications Commission as absorbed into the Department of Commerce and Labor to the Department of Justice in a manner prescribed by the Attorney General, and transfers corresponding empowerment of the Secretary of Commerce and Labor to the Attorney General.
The preexisting Federal Communications Commission text in this chapter is retained as enacted text; current USAR administration of the transferred functions is controlled by Pub. L. 36–256.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Patent and Trademark Administration
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(c), transfers in whole the functions of the former Patent and Trademark Office, together with the specified business-licensing, registration, branding, merchandising, and intellectual- or economic-property functions formerly assimilated into the Department of Commerce and Labor, to the Department of State under the direction of the Under Secretary of State for Management, or the Secretary of State when that office is vacant.
The preexisting organizational text of 35 U.S.C. § 1 is retained as enacted text; the later transfer governs current USAR administration.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Copyright Office
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 4(a), transfers the functions of the United States Copyright Office, including registration of copyrights, from the Library of Congress to the Department of State under the direction of the Under Secretary of State for Management, or the Secretary of State when that office is vacant.

Pub. L. 36–256, § 4(c), also transfers copyright-related empowerment of the Register of Copyrights or Librarian of Congress to the Under Secretary of State for Management, or the Secretary of State when that office is vacant or absent. The preexisting text is retained as enacted text subject to those later transfers.

notes.heading: USAR Transfer of Functions—Copyright Royalty Board
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 4(b), dissolves the Copyright Royalty Board and transfers its jurisdiction to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.
The preexisting Copyright Royalty Board provisions remain printed as enacted historical text, but the Board no longer exercises current USAR jurisdiction under Pub. L. 36–256.

notes.heading: USAR Functions Transferred to the Department of State
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(c), transfers former Patent and Trademark Office and specified licensing and intellectual-property functions to the Department of State; § 3(j) transfers to State any Department of Commerce and Labor function not otherwise transferred by the Act; and § 4(a) and (c) transfer Copyright Office functions and related copyright authority to State.

Pub. L. 38–265, § 3(k), subsequently defines the Bureau of Commerce and Labor as the Bureau under the authority of the Department of State, or a succeeding authority responsible for employment regulations. Sections 18A and 19 of Pub. L. 38–265 assign that Bureau administrative investigation, compliance-order, and civil-fine authority for the employment framework, subject to the limits stated in that Act.

notes.heading: USAR Functions Transferred to the Attorney General and Department of Justice
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(d), dissolves the Solicitor of Labor and absorbs that office into the Department of Justice. Section 3(e) transfers to Justice enforcement functions of the Department of Commerce and Labor not otherwise transferred; §§ 3(f)–(h) transfer the absorbed Federal Communications Commission, Federal Trade Commission, and National Labor Relations Board functions to Justice in a manner prescribed by the Attorney General.

The later Pub. L. 38–265 specifically assigns its employment-regulation administrative investigations, compliance orders, and civil fines to the State-side Bureau of Commerce and Labor. Under §§ 18A(d) and 19(f) of that Act, matters may be referred to the Department of Justice where criminal conduct or Justice enforcement is implicated.

notes.heading: USAR District of Columbia Jurisdiction—Transferred Commerce Functions
paragraphs: Pub. L. 36–256, § 3(i), provides that disputes in patents, trademarks, and other licensing registered by the Department of State under that Act are within the jurisdiction of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.
Pub. L. 36–256, § 4(b), separately dissolves the Copyright Royalty Board and transfers its jurisdiction to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.

notes.heading: USAR Federal Adverse-Action Framework
paragraphs: Pub. L. 38–265, §§ 10–15, establishes the current USAR federal-employment categories, career-employee adverse-action process, provisional-service rules, designated written at-will agreements, emergency-suspension authority, internal review, and direct judicial review in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.

Pub. L. 38–265, § 4(a), repeals the Federal Employment Reform Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 26–191); § 4(c) repeals the employment-separation framework of Pub. L. 21–123 to the extent specified; and § 4(e) supersedes prior law, regulation, executive order, policy, or procedure to the extent of inconsistency concerning resignation, termination, adverse-action process, or at-will status. Accordingly, inconsistent preexisting procedures in this section do not displace the later USAR framework for employment covered by Pub. L. 38–265.

notes.heading: USAR Dual-Employment and Conflict-of-Interest Limitation
paragraphs: Pub. L. 38–265, § 18, separately prohibits a federal employee from holding another federal position when the duties materially overlap or create a conflict of interest, and prohibits use of federal position for personal gain or an improper advantage to an affiliated private business.

Under § 18A, knowing or negligent violations constitute misconduct; agencies may order specified corrective action; the Bureau of Commerce and Labor may investigate and use § 19 compliance remedies; suspected fraud, bribery, theft, or other criminal conduct may be referred to the Department of Justice; and Title IV creates no private right of action. These restrictions operate independently of the dual-pay rules printed in this section.

notes.heading: USAR Private-Employment At-Will Framework
paragraphs: Pub. L. 38–265, §§ 7–9, establishes an at-will default for private employment: either party may terminate at any time, with or without cause or notice, except to the extent a written contract, collective-bargaining agreement, other written employment agreement, or other applicable law provides otherwise.

The Act preserves applicable prohibitions on unlawful discrimination and retaliation, including the cited federal civil-rights provisions, and does not create a general cause of action to challenge the fairness of an at-will termination. This is a cross-reference to the freestanding Pub. L. 38–265 framework and does not amend the Fair Labor Standards Act text of this chapter.

notes.heading: USAR Intelligence-Community Employment Framework
paragraphs: Pub. L. 38–265, § 4(b), repeals Pub. L. 28–204, the Intelligence Community Employment Act, and consolidates that subject matter into Title III of Pub. L. 38–265.

Under Pub. L. 38–265, § 16, sensitive intelligence positions are treated as at-will for removal, reassignment, or termination, subject to the Act's discrimination, retaliation, classified-record, and judicial-review safeguards; positions primarily engaged in criminal investigation are excluded from that at-will rule solely by virtue of Intelligence Community placement. Section 17 preserves agency control over classified access and limits review of the merits of classification and clearance decisions.

notes.heading: USAR Judicial Review Under the 2026 Employment Act
paragraphs: Pub. L. 38–265, § 15, authorizes a person aggrieved by final agency action under § 14 to seek judicial review in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia within seven days, under the scope and remedies specified by that Act.
Pub. L. 38–265, § 19(e), likewise provides expedited District of Columbia review of Bureau compliance orders and civil fines within the Act's stated seven-day period, subject to § 22.
